# The Moment of Revelation

> "Our soul has escaped like a bird out of the fowler's snare. The snare is broken, and we have escaped."
>
> — Psalm 124:7

Some time in the first three weeks after he stops, a man usually has what this method calls the moment of revelation.

It's hard to describe and you can't mistake it. The day looks brighter. Up to then you've been *telling* yourself that you don't need the habit. In this moment you find you no longer have to tell yourself anything. The last thread has gone. You know you're done with it, and you don't want it back. From then on you look at men who are still in the trap and feel only pity.

One of the Psalms has a picture of it. "Our soul has escaped like a bird out of the fowler's snare." A fowler is a man who traps birds. The bird is out, and the snare lies broken on the ground behind it. The next line says who broke it: "Our help is in the LORD's name, who made heaven and earth."

Men who stop by willpower rarely get this moment. They're glad they've stopped, but they go through life believing they gave something up, so there's never a day when the weight comes off.

The deeper in you were, the better the moment is, and it doesn't wear off. Most joys fade. You remember that your wedding day or your first paycheck was wonderful, but you can't call the feeling back. This one you can. On a gray afternoon years from now you'll be able to stop and think, "I don't do that anymore," and feel glad again.

## When does it come? {-}

For most men it's days, not weeks.

For the man in Chapter 21 it came on the first day. With some readers it happens before the book is finished. Somewhere in the middle chapters they put it down and say, "That's enough. I can see the whole thing. I'm done." Readers of EasyPeasy report the same about porn. One, twelve days out, had already stopped thinking of himself as a man holding on: "I just refer to myself as 'nonuser'", he wrote, and "I feel much happier as nonuser."

And let's be honest that it doesn't come to every man as a moment. For some it's sudden, a single day they can name. For others it comes on like a dawn. One young man, telling how God freed him, was careful to say so: "this wasn't something that happened overnight". Both kinds are real, and the slow kind is no less free. If yours comes by degrees, you haven't done it wrong. So take the two figures below as a rough guide and no more. They are not a sentence to serve, and they are not a date to wait for.

**About five days in,** the habit stops being the main thing on your mind. This is when most men have their moment. It usually comes in one of the old danger spots: the empty house, the sleepless night, the evening after a fight. You get to the far side of it and suddenly realize that you coped perfectly well, or even enjoyed yourself. The thought of the habit never crossed your mind. After that it's smooth sailing, and you know you're free.

**About three weeks in** is when most willpower attempts die, and it's worth knowing why.

## The three-week trap {-}

By the third week the man senses that the desire has gone. He isn't sure, so he decides to prove it. "I'll just see. If it does nothing for me, I'll know I've beaten it."

And it does feel odd. It's flat and a bit silly, and he takes that as his proof. But he has just handed the Little Monster its first meal in three weeks. Within the hour a small voice starts up: "You haven't beaten it. You want another."

He doesn't go straight back, because he's no fool and doesn't want to get hooked. He lets a safe-looking gap go by. Then the next temptation comes, and this time he has an answer ready: "I did it once and didn't get hooked. So where's the harm?"

He's already on the slope.

So don't prove anything to anyone, including yourself. You will never need to test your freedom, and every test of it is the habit under another name.

## Don't wait for it {-}

The answer is not to sit waiting for the moment of revelation. The answer is to see that it's finished from the moment you decide. You've cut off the Little Monster's supply. Nothing on earth can stop you being free now, unless you sit moping or wait for a sign.

If you're a Christian you have firmer ground than a feeling. Paul says that if anyone is in Christ, "he is a new creation. The old things have passed away." He wrote that as a fact about you, and the feeling will catch up with the fact.

So go and enjoy your life, and cope with it, from the very start.

The moment will arrive soon enough.

One short chapter comes before the final step. It is more serious than this one, because it is about what you are being freed for.
